summary: Autonomous driving is the visible front, but AI runs through freight matching, maritime navigation, transit operations, and aviation. Who tracks it: the safety regulators and standards bodies are the primary record, with the operators' own published data layered on top.

analysis.body:
Per the Census Bureau, 11.2 percent of transportation and warehousing firms reported using AI in the latest survey period, up from 10.7 percent in the prior period, suggesting measured but gradual uptake across a sector that spans trucking, aviation, maritime, and freight brokerage.

The most visible application is autonomous trucking, where Aurora has deployed its Aurora Driver on commercial highway corridors, with partners including Werner citing the system's ability to autonomously haul freight between Fort Worth and El Paso. Aurora's operator partners describe early pilot results as impressive and point to projected fivefold freight volume growth between 2010 and 2050 as a structural argument for autonomous transport. In ride-hailing, Waymo traces its lineage to the Google Self-Driving Car Project, founded in 2009, and frames its deployment as a direct response to what it describes as an unacceptable status quo in road safety, publishing a comprehensive safety program and crash-rate methodology as its public evidence base.

Fleet telematics represents AI at broad commercial scale today. Samsara reports that its AI-powered dash cams, real-time in-cab alerts, and automated coaching technologies have contributed to more than 380,000 accidents prevented across more than 20,000 operations, with capabilities including drowsiness detection and predictive analytics for risk and maintenance. In freight brokerage, C.H. Robinson describes a shift toward what it calls autonomous logistics orchestration, where supply chains analyze, decide, execute, and improve continuously across every shipment, applying AI to load matching and route optimization across one of the largest third-party logistics networks.

In maritime, Wärtsilä positions AI-driven predictive analytics as part of its decarbonization toolkit for the marine market, running alongside engines designed for low- and zero-carbon fuels. The International Maritime Organization adopted a new International Code of Safety for Maritime Autonomous Surface Ships in May 2026, which came into effect on 1 July 2026, establishing a goal-based framework for design, construction, operation, and certification of autonomous vessels. The IMO notes that at present there are no commercially operating, internationally trading SOLAS cargo ships that operate autonomously or under remote control, though successful trials have demonstrated feasibility and commercial entry may follow. In aviation, Airbus frames its innovation work around a decarbonized, connected, and autonomous future for aerospace, while EASA has published its Artificial Intelligence Roadmap 2.0, a living document updated annually that sets out safety and ethical considerations and anticipates future rulemaking, meaning nothing reaches commercial flight without passing through that regulatory gate.

For a decision-maker considering deployment, the sector presents a clear split between applications that are commercially live and those still working through certification. Telematics-based AI, freight matching, and predictive maintenance are available now and carry documented safety and efficiency evidence. Fully autonomous vehicles, crewless vessels, and AI flight systems face regulatory timelines set by the American Trucking Associations' policy environment, the IMO's MASS Code transition from voluntary to mandatory instrument, and EASA's incremental rulemaking calendar, all of which reward early engagement with standards processes as much as early investment in the technology itself.
